title: In Search of Perfection: aci-cpp vs. llama.cpp v1.0.0
content:
In Search of Perfection: aci-cpp vs. llama.cpp v1.0.0
Heston Blumenthal is the head chef of The Fat Duck, a restaurant in the UK which for some amount of years has changed the underlying structure of fine dining. He had a show a few years back on the BBC network called “In Search of Perfection”. He’d use calipers to measure people’s jaws to find out the perfect size of a cheeseburger based on the clearance of the average person’s bite, spend months trying to figure out how to make his own processed American cheese from reverse engineering McDonalds quarter pounders, combining all sorts of different optimizations derived from studying the form of anything he was seeking to ultimately make perfect.
At Actual, we are similarly chasing perfection in our own domain, especially in how we develop our ex-nihilo flagship engine, e. Today, we’re sharing improvements we’ve made using the same development processes to llama.cpp: aci-cpp is our oldest engine, which we have continuously improved since we first gave users access to the platform. Here’s what we’ve accomplished, and where we're taking it in the future.
What's aci-cpp?
aci-cpp is our fork of llama.cpp. It's the engine the Actual client runs on Macs, on machines like the DGX Spark, on consumer Nvidia cards, and tons of other hardware. llama.cpp is one of the best pieces of open-source software ever created, and we build on it rather than around it. Where upstream ships a better kernel, we take it. Where our users' workloads need something upstream doesn't do yet, we write it.
The client now ships aci-cpp 7e2590782a. Below, we compare it with llama.cpp v1.0.0, the upstream release, on Qwen3.8-27B at Q4_K_M, a model many of you run.
How fast is the next turn?
Agents and long chats spend most of their life on the second turn and beyond: a long conversation is already in memory, a few hundred new tokens arrive, and you're waiting for the first word back.
On a DGX Spark, aci-cpp answers a follow-up turn 17% to 28% faster than llama.cpp v1.0.0, from 8K to 250K tokens of context. With 64K tokens in context, the first token comes back in 0.78 seconds instead of 0.97. With 250K, it's 1.79 seconds instead of 2.10.
Our previous build took 5.2 seconds at 250K. This one takes 1.79.
How much can one DGX Spark serve?
Serving many streams at once, aci-cpp delivers 6% to 25% more total throughput than llama.cpp v1.0.0 on 512-token prompts, and 19% to 37% more on 4,096-token prompts, from 2 to 16 concurrent streams.
We also ran the same grid against upstream's latest development build, which has its own multi-token prediction (MTP). With speculation off in both, aci-cpp led in every cell. With MTP on in both, our drafter beat upstream's MTP by 4% to 38% in every cell.
What about long context on a Mac?
Long context is where Macs used to struggle. Reading a quarter-million tokens of memory for every new word puts real pressure on the memory system.
On an M3 Ultra with 250K tokens in context, aci-cpp now decodes at 12.6 tokens per second, 46% faster than our previous client build, and slightly ahead of llama.cpp v1.0.0 at every depth we measured, from 8K to 250K.
Under many streams, the M3 Ultra serves 16% to 26% more tokens per second than v1.0.0 on 512-token prompts. On an M2 Ultra, batched decode runs up to 34% faster at 32 streams, and served throughput on 512-token prompts is 6% to 8% higher.
Where do we stand?
Here's every platform and workload we measured against llama.cpp v1.0.0, side by side.
aci-cpp is ahead of llama.cpp v1.0.0 on eight of the ten workloads, by up to 28%, and within 1% on the other two.
What did we change?
Sixty merged performance changes since we opened the platform. A few themes:
- Prefill on NVIDIA. New int8 tensor-core matrix multiplies read GGUF weights in place. On the DGX Spark, prompt processing at 2,048 tokens got 27% faster on Q4_K_M and about 31% faster on Q8_0, each measured against our own previous build. RTX Blackwell cards got the same family of kernels.
- Qwen3.8's linear-attention layers. Fused, chunked kernels for the gated DeltaNet on CUDA and Metal, for both prefill and decode.
- Speculative decoding. A faster MTP drafter, and few-row matrix multiplies that verify several draft tokens for about the cost of one.
- Long context. Flash attention that skips masked blocks, per-sequence KV blocks in shared caches, and a row-list read path for very long KV spans on the M3 Ultra.
- Serving. Prefill scheduled by token budget across slots, parallel sampling, and faster prompt-cache saves.
How we measured
Every number here is measured in our lab on Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M, alternating builds on the same machine; each chart notes its conditions.
Our belief at Actual is that token efficiency should only be bounded by the physical limitations of the hardware, and not by trade-offs within the software. Ultimately, allowing you -- the Actual user -- to get more tokens of the same quality out of the hardware you already own is our idea of achieving this goal. We couldn't do it without you. Every email, bug report, or DM our employees receive has been critical for our ability to build this for you, and we can't thank you enough for your support.
For you, we will keep chasing perfection.
Install Actual
Run AI on your own computers. One command installs Actual; then authorize the device at the actual.inc/device link it prints.

report.summary: Actual's aci-cpp fork beats llama.cpp v1.0.0 on 8 of 10 benchmarks by up to 28%, with big long-context and serving gains on DGX Spark and Macs.
report.background: llama.cpp began in 2023 as Georgi Gerganov's weekend hack to run LLaMA models on consumer hardware and quickly became the de facto open-source engine for local inference, defining the GGUF weight format and powering tools like Ollama and LM Studio. Its recent v1.0.0 release marks a maturity milestone for the project. Meanwhile, hardware has shifted: Nvidia's DGX Spark puts a Grace Blackwell chip on a desk, and Apple Silicon's unified memory made Macs a favorite for large-context local models. With model quality converging, competition has moved to inference efficiency — prefill speed, decode latency on long conversations, speculative decoding, KV-cache management, and batched multi-stream serving. Actual, a startup building a local AI client, maintains aci-cpp, a long-running fork of llama.cpp that it tunes for its users' workloads while pulling in upstream improvements.
key_points: Follow-up turn latency is the headline win: on a DGX Spark, aci-cpp returns the first token 17% to 28% faster than llama.cpp v1.0.0 across 8K to 250K tokens of context. At 64K context that is 0.78s versus 0.97s; at 250K it is 1.79s versus 2.10s, down from 5.2s in Actual's previous build.

Multi-stream serving improves too: 6% to 25% more total throughput on 512-token prompts and 19% to 37% more on 4,096-token prompts across 2 to 16 concurrent streams. Against upstream's development build with its own multi-token prediction, aci-cpp's drafter still led by 4% to 38% with speculation enabled on both.

Long context on Apple Silicon got the biggest single jump: an M3 Ultra decoding with 250K tokens in context now hits 12.6 tokens per second, 46% faster than Actual's prior build and slightly ahead of v1.0.0 at every depth. On an M2 Ultra, batched decode runs up to 34% faster at 32 streams.

Roughly sixty merged performance changes underlie this: int8 tensor-core matmuls that read GGUF weights in place, fused chunked kernels for Qwen3.8's gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers on CUDA and Metal, a faster speculative drafter with few-row matmuls that verify several draft tokens for near the cost of one, flash attention that skips masked blocks, per-sequence KV blocks in shared caches, and token-budget prefill scheduling.

The bottom line: aci-cpp leads on eight of ten measured workloads by up to 28% and is within 1% on the other two. Actual frames the goal as token efficiency bounded only by hardware physics, not software trade-offs — though all numbers are vendor-run lab benchmarks on a single model, Qwen3.8-27B at Q4_K_M.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals that local inference is now a genuine performance race, and that downstream forks can out-accelerate the upstream project they depend on — raising familiar open-source questions about whether such optimizations get upstreamed or fragment the ecosystem. For developers, the specific techniques (in-place int8 tensor-core reads of GGUF weights, fused DeltaNet kernels, cheap multi-token verification, masked-block-skipping attention, per-sequence KV blocks) are broadly applicable and worth studying even outside this fork. For regular users, the practical payoff is snappier follow-up turns in long chats, usable quarter-million-token contexts on a single Mac or desk-side box, and better local serving for small teams. Caveats: benchmarks are vendor-run on one model and one quantization, and committing to a fork carries compatibility and maintenance risk.
report.tools: Start with llama.cpp itself and its GGUF format; Actual's client is the reference implementation of aci-cpp. For comparison, try Ollama and LM Studio (both llama.cpp-based, user-friendly), vLLM for high-throughput GPU serving, Apple's MLX for Mac-native work, and MLC-LLM for compiled deployment. If you want to verify claims, rerun the Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M grid on your own DGX Spark or M-series Mac, and watch upstream llama.cpp PRs to see which of these optimizations land.
